newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines, pilots to meet as strike looms.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines, pilots to meet as strike looms.

text.p: American Airlines and its pilots' union, at loggerheads over a new labor contract, are to meet Monday for round-the-clock negotiations aimed at staving off a devastating strike at the nation's No. 2 carrier.
With the Allied Pilots Association pledging to shut down the airline at midnight Friday, Feb. 14 if no deal is reached by then, the stakes are high.
Management has warned a strike could wreck the company but says that accepting the pilots' demands would kill its chances of competing against lower-cost rivals.
"We are faced with two disastrous alternatives -- unacceptably high costs or cessation of operations," Chief Executive Officer Robert Crandall told employees in a recent letter.

Most of the 90,000 employees at American Airlines, its commuter carrier American Eagle and parent company AMR Corp. would be placed on unpaid "emergency leave" as soon as a strike begins and the stoppage could cause havoc at airports across the country, especially in Dallas, Chicago, Los Angeles, Miami and New York.
American, which is based in Fort Worth, Texas, carries about 200,000 passengers on domestic U.S. flights every day, nearly 20 percent of the total.

A strike would cost the airline an estimated $1 billion per month. American said last week it was drawing $1 billion from an existing credit line and has arranged to borrow another $1 billion under a new credit agreement if needed.
Pilots' union leaders say they hope this week's talks in Washington will bring agreement but insist they will have no hesitation in ordering a walkout if the company does not meet their demands.
They want pay raises worth about 11.5 percent over the life of a four-year contract, while the airline has so far offered just 5 percent.

Another key issue is the use of regional jets. Crandall wants to equip American Eagle with 50-passenger jets to handle short-haul routes but the APA is bitterly opposed and accuses him of trying to transfer routes -- and its members' jobs -- to the lower-cost commuter carrier, which employs pilots from another union and currently only flies turboprop aircraft.

American has called on the pilots to accept binding arbitration in the contract dispute, which began in 1994, but APA president Jim Sovich says his members want a deal now and are willing to shut down the airline rather than risk lengthy arbitration in order to get it.
So American has turned to Congress for help, urging lawmakers to back up its push for arbitraton.
On Friday, all 17 members of the Senate Aviation Subcommittee called on President Clinton to help mediate a settlement or move it to arbitration before a strike begins.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the administration was ready to help, but indicated Clinton would not intervene unless asked to do so by both sides.
"I think both parties would have to see a constructive role for us to play in order for us to be useful," McCurry said.
In 1993, Clinton ended a five-day strike by American Airlines flight attendants by persuading Crandall to submit the dispute to arbitration.
Pilots' union leaders have indicated they would not welcome such a move this time around.

One senior union official said he thinks the chances of a strike beginning midnight Friday are 50-50 but added that the two sides, although far apart, could still bridge the gap at the negotiating table.
"You never know what is going to happen once you sit down. There could be some new proposals and some creative thinking. That's what you hope for anyway," he said.
The negotiations, to be held at a Washington hotel, will be mediated by the National Mediation Board.
Crandall, who has bad relations with pilots' union leaders, will not participate directly in the negotiations so American's team will be led by airline president Don Carty.
